div.head: La fonction de la hanche et les caractéristiques du swing diffèrent chez les golfeurs ayant ou non des antécédents de lombalgie
Introduction
div.p: Low back pain (LBP) has been identified as a prevalent condition among athletes, with a particularly high incidence observed in sports that involve repetitive trunk rotation, such as golf [1]. Robinson et al. conducted a prospective study of injury incidence in over 900 amateur golfers, revealing that lumbosacral injuries were the most common [2].

The golf swing is a complex whole-body motion that requires coordinated movements of the lower extremities, pelvis, spine, and upper extremities, among others [3]. A number of factors have been identified as being associated with LBP in golfers. These factors include age, a history of LBP, body weight, repeated incorrect swing biomechanics, excessive physical activity, and poor physical function [1]. A study of physical function in golfers concluded that factors associated with LBP include impairment of hip internal rotation (IR) range of motion (ROM) and trunk muscle weakness [4][5][6]. These factors have also been identified in patients with LBP outside of golf [7][8][9][10]. Further support for the association between LBP and hip muscle strength in golfers, is shown by the identification of weakness of the lead-side hip abductor and adductor muscle groups in LBP [11]. Despite this evidence no studies have comprehensively examined hip flexibility and strength as factors in golf associated LBP.

A number of issues have been identified in the biomechanics of the golf swing, which is associated with the presence of LBP. The ''Address'' angle is defined as the body position immediately before striking the ball. A study revealed that at the Address position golfers complaining of LBP exhibited diminished knee joint flexion and ankle dorsiflexion angle in comparison to golfers without LBP. The investigation revealed that the spine angles at Address did not exhibit significant disparities between the groups with and without LBP [12]. During the golf swing, golfers with LBP had decreased maximum whole trunk right rotation ROM and increased maximum whole spine left lateral flexion ROM. Other reports have reported varied results [11,13]. One explanation for this is that previous studies have only evaluated the entire spine as a unit and do not reveal the detailed behavior of the lumbar spine. When evaluating LBP, it would be useful to know what is happening in the lumbar spine, the presumed nociceptive source of pain. A more comprehensive evaluation of the lumbar spine's maximum ROM during the golf swing may offer novel insights into LBP in golf. The objective of this pilot study was to identify differences in hip flexibility, hip muscle strength, and golf swing motion in amateur golfers with and without LBP. The present study will examine the role of the hip and lumbar spine in LBP for golfers and provide fundamental data for future studies aimed at identifying prevention and treatment methods for this population.

div.head: Participants
div.p: Participants were recruited through posters displayed at four golf driving ranges from May to November 2021. Prior to the commencement of the measurement process, participants were required to provide written consent. Inclusion criteria were that they had no current symptoms of LBP and were not currently receiving hospital treatment for their condition. Furthermore, subjects were required to have participated in a minimum of five rounds of golf, with a maximum score of 110 or less over 18 holes. A paper questionnaire was administered to collect data on subjects' height, weight, golf scores, and history of LBP due to golf. It is noteworthy that the subjects with LBP were included if they experienced LBP exclusively while golfing, and were excluded if LBP occurred in daily life or in another sport.

div.head: Hip joint function assessment
div.p: Passive hip IR and external rotation (ER) ROM was measured using an inclinometer placed on the prone subjects shin, with their hip positioned in mid adduction/abduction and their knee flexed to 90 • . This measurement method has been reported to have high intra-and inter-examiner reliability [14]. Hamstring and hip flexor muscle extensibility was evaluated by the straight leg raise (SLR) and Thomas test respectively. For the SLR test, the subject lay supine, an inclinometer was placed on their shin and used to record SLR ROM. The measurement of SLR was obtained with their knee held in extension and their hip passively flexed to maximum range. Extensibility of the hip flexor muscles was determined by the Thomas test where contralateral hip flexion ROM was recorded while the subject's opposite hip was maintained in maximal flexion. Compensatory movement of pelvic rotation was corrected by the examiner. Intra-individual variability of the SLR test and Thomas test was determined by ICC (1,3). All values were above 0.9, indicating excellent reliability. ROM and flexibility tests were measured three times, and the average value used for measurements. Hip isometric muscle strength was measured using a hand-held dynamometer. Two parameters were evaluated: IR and ER. Replicating previous studies, strength measurements were evaluated in a seated position and all muscle strength measurements taken twice [15].

div.head: Golf swing analysis
div.p: The golf swing was measured using a three-dimensional motion analyzer (Vicon MX System; Vicon Motion Systems Ltd., Oxford, UK). A Plug-in-Gait AI model was used to calculate the lower limb kinematic data. Additionally, ten markers were added to measure spine motion. This set of markers can be used to separate the upper and lower lumbar spine and calculate data for the lumbar spine [16]. The upper lumbar spine was defined as L1 to L3, and the lower lumbar spine as L4 to L5. Lumbar spine motion data were calculated using Visual 3D (C-Motion, Germantown, MD, USA). The sampling frequency was set at 240 Hz, while the cutoff frequency was 6 Hz. During data collection participants performed the golf swing with their own golf clubs, shoes, and gloves. Prior to the initiation of the golf swing measurements, the participants engaged in a three-minute warm-up period during which they were permitted to swing the golf club with any intensity and method they deemed appropriate. The measurement process involved the use of a driver and the execution of five full swings. The participants were instructed to imagine that they were situated on a golf tee and they should attempt to strike the ball towards a net positioned approximately three meters in front of them. The data from three of the five successful golf swing trials were used to calculate the average values. The data from the latter three was primarily utilized. In instances where data accuracy was deemed inadequate, data from the first or second was adopted. For right-handed golfers, the left side was designated as the lead side, and the right side was designated as the trail side. The posture of the golf swing prior to the movement of the golf club was defined as Address. The angles of the hip joints and the upper and lower lumbar spine were calculated. The maximum range during the golf swing was calculated for both hip IR as well as lateral flexion, rotation, and extension of the upper and lower lumbar spine.

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: Normality of the data was determined. For each measurement item, independent t-tests or Mann-Whitney U-tests were employed, depending on the statistical assumptions of the test. The calculation of effect sizes and power was conducted for all test results. The calculation of effect sizes employed Cohen's d for the independent t-test and effect size r for the Mann-Whitney U-test. The statistical software utilized was IBM SPSS Statistics for Mac, version 29.0 (Armonk, NY, USA: IBM Corp 2020). A significance level of P < 0.05 was employed.

div.head: Results
div.p: The demographic characteristics of the participants are shown in Table 1. All participants were right-handed with 9 in the LBP group and 13 in the Non-LBP group. A subsequent analysis revealed that there was no statistically significant difference in the basic demographics between the two groups (P > 0.05). Table 2 presents the hip joint function characteristics of the 2 groups. There were no statistically significant differences in hip IR and ER ROM, or ROM on the SLR or Thomas test (P > 0.05). However, a statistically significant difference was observed in hip ER strength, with the LBP group exhibiting lower strength compared to the Non-LBP group (P < 0.05). Tables 3 and 4 present the three-dimensional motion analysis data for the hip and lumbar spine, respectively. At Address significantly higher values were noted for the LBP group in both left and right side hip flexion angle (P < 0.05). Furthermore, the upper lumbar spine left-right rotation maximum ROM during the golf swing was found to be significantly higher in the LBP

div.head: Discussion
div.p: The objective of this study was to identify potential disparities in hip joint function and golf swing parameters among golfers with LBP compared to those without pain. The investigation yielded several noteworthy findings. Significantly lower hip ER muscle strength was observed in the LBP group. Furthermore, the LBP group exhibited significantly greater upper lumbar spine left and right rotation ROM during the golf swing. Similar studies have reported that individuals with LBP exhibit reduced hip muscle strength compared to those without LBP [9], and LBP has been associated with atrophy of the gluteus maximus muscle [17,18]. Hip ER muscle force generated during the golf swing is greater in the forward swing phase on the lead side and in the acceleration phase on the trail side [19]. These phases are of importance in accelerating the golf club and generating ball carry distance. It is reported that golf driving distance is more closely correlated with hip muscle strength than trunk core muscle strength [20]. This would infer that the hip ER muscles are important for the golf swing. It has been hypothesized that individuals who suffer with LBP may have sought to enhance their golf performance by employing greater lumbar rotation movement to compensate for diminished strength in both left and right side hip ER muscle groups. Consequently, it can be considered potentially important to incorporate the hip ER muscle group into the evaluation and rehabilitation framework for golfers with LBP. A previous study similarly identified the hip and trunk muscle function as important for golfers with LBP [11].

To the best of our knowledge, there is no difference in lumbar kyphosis angle or pelvic tilt angle between golfers with and without LBP [9]. Furthermore, no significant difference in hip or spine angle has been reported at the golf swing position Address [12]. However, a notable finding in our study was a significant increase in hip flexion angle at Address observed in the LBP group. We consider this observation as an important finding of our study, however the underlying reasons for the distinctive posture at Address in golfers with LBP remains to be determined.

It has been shown that the gluteus maximus muscles undergo both stretching and increased muscle activity when the hip joint is flexed [21]. This finding suggests that one of the characteristics of the altered Address position in the LBP group may be as a compensatory mechanism due to a decrease in hip ER muscle strength. Additionally, it has been documented that golfers with LBP exhibit a significantly faster onset of the erector spinae muscle activation during the back swing and with greater muscle activity [22]. This phenomenon could be attributed to the increased hip flexion angle, which has been observed to stretch the erector spinae muscles, thereby potentially augmenting the load on these muscles. In light of these considerations, it would appear to be useful to educate golfers who have experienced LBP about their altered Address posture.

No substantial differences were identified between groups with respect to hip IR and ER ROM, SLR test ROM, and Thomas test ROM outcomes. A well-documented risk factor for LBP is reduced flexibility of the hip muscles, including hamstrings and iliopsoas muscles [7,8,23]. Golf is a sport requiring predominantly trunk and pelvis rotation. Consequently, the flexibility of the aforementioned muscles, while important limiting factors in hip flexion and extension, may not have a substantial impact on the load on the lumbar spine during the golf swing.

Previous reports have indicated that golfers with LBP demonstrate diminished hip IR ROM [5,6]. Given the established correlation between diminished hip IR ROM and augmented lumbar rotation ROM [24], a plausible hypothesis is proposed that links LBP and hip IR ROM in golf. However, the findings of our study did not demonstrate such a correlation. The discrepancy between the findings of our study and those previous ones may be attributed to the distinct characteristics of the participants in the two studies, particularly their varying levels of competitive engagement. In contrast, Kim et al.'s study focused on young professional golfers. In contrast, the present study's participants were amateur golfers. It has been documented that the golf swing movement style varies according to the level of competition [25]. Consequently, it was proposed that varying levels of competition may be associated with distinct factors contributing to LBP.

Although this study does not establish a causal relationship between LBP and hip function, the findings provide clinically relevant implications for sports medicine. The assessment of hip ER muscle strength, posture at Address, and excessive upper lumbar spine rotation ROM during the golf swing may serve as useful screening items in clinical and field settings. For golfers with a history of LBP, monitoring these checkpoints may potentially help reduce lumbar load, prevent recurrence of injury, and support the maintenance of competitive performance.

The present study is not without its limitations. Firstly, the nature of this study, being cross-sectional and observational, precludes the establishment of a clear causal relationship between LBP and hip joint function. Future studies should employ longitudinal research designs to more thoroughly examine the interaction between LBP and hip joint function. Secondly, the study did not include data on muscle activity, center of gravity position, and ground reaction force during the golf swing. Consequently, the investigation of how these factors were influenced by LBP was precluded. These data may offer insights into the underlying mechanisms of LBP and should be considered in future studies. Thirdly, the study's participants were limited to amateur golfers, and the external validity of the results for professional golfers and players with higher levels of competition is unclear.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This study demonstrated an association between LBP and specific physical characteristics and golf swing mechanics in amateur golfers. Golfers with LBP demonstrated increased hip flexion angles during the Address position and greater upper lumbar spine rotation ROM during the golf swing compared to golfers without LBP. Furthermore, reduced hip ER muscle strength was observed in golfers with LBP, suggesting the presence of compensatory movement patterns and physical characteristics that may contribute to LBP. The cross-sectional design and the participants' characteristics of this study limit the ability to establish causal relationships between LBP and its associated factors. However, the findings highlight the potential importance of addressing hip function and golf swing mechanics in golfers with LBP. Consequently, therapists and instructors may benefit from assessing hip ER muscle strength, Address position, and excessive lumbar rotation ROM during the golf swing to reduce LBP in amateur golfers.
